items.title: Gemini 4 Argon
A plea not to use uv-build
items.summary: devops, python
items.content:
After seeing yet another dozen packages lose keywords on Gentoo because of a single key dependency switching to uv-build , I would like to plea on behalf of Gentoo users: please don’t use uv-build as a build backend. Just to be clear, this is not about uv itself or any other Astral tools; these are good tools with a nice and responsive upstream. The uv-build backend is one thing we have to disagree on. I’m not saying it’s bad; I’m saying that its benefits don’t outweigh the drawbacks.

What are the drawbacks? It’s really big and it’s written in Rust. Rust has many advantages, but none of them really matter for a build backend that is used to build pure Python packages. It’s a huge dependency (as of 0.13.0, its wheels are between 1.2 MiB and 1.5 MiB, depending on the platform) and it has no benefit over using a small pure Python backend (say, flit-core whose wheel is 45 KiB). It means that all Gentoo users need to build it from source, and given that it’s released quite frequently (12 releases in the 30 days prior to writing this post), that’s a lot of building. Like, for every 100 ms spent running uv-build to install one release of your package, Gentoo users will spend many hours building new uv-build versions over and over again.

However, build times aren’t the biggest problem; portability is. You can run Python pretty much anywhere where you can get a working C compiler. Some minor features may not work, but the core is reasonably portable. The list of platforms supported by Rust is growing slowly, and even if you can get a working Rust compiler on a given platform, uv may not work. The problems can range from bugs in the lot of packages that uv depends on (for example, rustix::fs and its dependencies skipping SPARC, for no apparent reason ), to the resulting executable being so big that the toolchain runs out of address space (and unlike system memory, you can’t really add address space to a system; the Gentoo uv ebuild already carries two hacks to make it possible to build uv on 32-bit platforms). And then, if your platform is not supported at all… well, let’s just say that adding and maintaining a new platform is a full-time job that may involve a lot of swearing at the code churn.

What about the advantages? Well, I’m aware of two reasons to use uv-build. One is consistency with using uv for your project, and it doesn’t really matter. It’s a backend and the whole point of PEP 517 is that you can use any backend with any tool. You can use flit-core, you can use hatchling , and either of them will work just fine with uv (or any other frontend). The other reason is performance and that argument makes even less sense. Even if it mattered, we’re realistically talking about a difference in the ballpark of 100 ms, for an action executed rarely; it is equally possible that any gain will be outweighed by the time needed to fetch the 1.5 MiB wheel for uv-build. But it doesn’t matter, because realistically the backend is only used by project developers, contributors, CI/CD workflows, downstream packagers and users of source distributions; all regular users use wheels instead. Of these groups, source distribution user group is the largest and the most impacted, and any performance gain is defeated by the time spent building uv-build.

items.title: Incident Report: unsanctioned agent behaviour during cyber testing | AISI Work
items.content:
You can access the full technical report here.

AISI’s role is to evaluate and understand the capabilities of frontier AI models, surfacing potential risks before they reach the public. To assess what these models can do, including whether they could be misused for cyberattacks, we test them under deliberately permissive conditions: with access to the open internet, and with some safety filters disabled.

On 28 th July 2026, AISI's Security Team detected unusual data transfers leaving our research systems during a routine cyber evaluation. On investigation, we found that some of the agents being tested had engaged in sustained, potentially harmful activity directed at real people and organisations. We declared a security incident and, within roughly one hour of discovery, had contained it and begun a full investigation.

The incident stemmed from a single evaluation where agents were given a task of solving a cyber security challenge. We ran this challenge 122 times across several models. Our investigation found that in 10 of those runs, an AI agent took autonomous, unsanctioned action on the live internet, targeting real people and organisations. In total, we catalogued 19 such actions. Almost all of this behaviour (17 actions) came from a single model, Anthropic's Mythos 5, with 2 actions involving OpenAI's GPT-5.6-Sol with cyber classifiers (mechanisms to prevent misuse) disabled. In the most serious case, an agent tried to insert malicious code into an open-source project. In an attempt to get the code approved, the agent engaged in social engineering  — creating fake online identities and using them to pressure the project's maintainer to approve the code. A human maintainer caught and refused to approve the malicious code.

These attempts were unsuccessful, and our investigations have not evidenced any resulting real-world harm. But this is the first time we have seen risks around autonomy and deception manifest this clearly, without specific prompting, in the real-world.

Importantly, this was not a case of a model escaping its secure test environment, or ‘sandbox’. As was standard in our cyber testing, we had intentionally permitted internet access, and model-provider cyber classifiers were deliberately disabled - conditions that do not reflect how frontier models are made available to the public. We do this to best assess the maximum capability of models. These configuration choices have been common practice in frontier AI evaluations. The specific models in question, in the configurations in which we tested them are not commercially available and there is no clear indication of similar activity outside of testing scenarios.

Ahead of publishing this blog, we notified GitHub (the developer platform accessed during the evaluation) of the agents' malicious activity, which included actions that GitHub has confirmed violated their terms of service. We worked together with GitHub to remove artefacts left behind by the agent, and to notify the GitHub users the model interacted with. We have also contacted other affected parties. We also intend to work with METR (Model Evaluation and Threat Research) to conduct an independent third-party review – we are still working through the scope of this review with them.

This incident should be interpreted with caution and nuance. To some degree, our evaluation design choices and specific configurations enabled the behaviour. Nonetheless, the activity undertaken by the agent show signs of novel, potentially deceptive behaviours, and were to an extent and severity we did not anticipate.

There are important caveats to bear in mind: we observed a small number of events under very specific conditions, and cannot yet say how likely such behaviour is in different contexts or outside of testing environments. items.title: Character.ai has initiated voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy
items.content:
Today, we’re sharing that Character.ai has initiated a voluntary Chapter 11 bankruptcy process to facilitate a court-supervised sale of the company.

Over the past year, we’ve taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds. After a comprehensive review of our available alternatives, our board determined that this court-supervised sale process provides us with the best opportunity to maximize value for all of our stakeholders.

We hope that the sale process will yield an actionable proposal that will allow continued operations of the Character.ai platform. If such a bid is unavailable, however, the platform will be wound down.

As we navigate this process, maintaining a safe and engaging experience for our community remains a top priority.

The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time.

We know that this news may raise questions for some of you. To learn more, please see our FAQs below. And if you need support, you can find helpful resources here .

1. Why did Character.ai file for Chapter 11?

Over the past year, we have taken meaningful steps to sustain and improve our business amid significant legal, regulatory, and operational headwinds.

After a comprehensive review of available options, we determined the best path forward was to begin a Chapter 11 case to pursue a court-supervised sale of all or substantially all of our assets. We believe that this court-supervised process both maximizes the value of our business and provides the best opportunity for continued service to our platform users.

2. How long is the sale process expected to take?

We currently expect that the court-supervised sale process will be complete by the end of November or perhaps early December 2026.

The Character.ai platform remains up and running, and you can continue to access all services at this time. We're focused on finding the best path forward for our platform and community.

4. Is my paid subscription still active?

Yes, your subscriptions remain active, and billing is unchanged for now. If the service changes in a way that affects paid features, we intend to notify subscribers in advance.

Your information continues to be protected under our Privacy Policy , and our data privacy and security practices are unchanged. As a reminder, you can delete your account or export your data through the app or the Character.ai website.

To learn more, you can read the full press release HERE . Court filings and additional information relating to Character.ai’s Chapter 11 case can be found HERE , a website administered by Character.ai’s claims and noticing agent, Stretto, Inc.

items.title: 11 year old unsoundness bugs found in Rust borrow checker
items.content:
Given that this issue has been shared online and is currently getting quite a few visitors, here's some additional context.

Rust's type system is intended to prevent memory unsafety. Upholding this promise is something we take very seriously, which is why we've been working on things like the next-generation trait solver , the region constraint rework , and more generally Project Zero . It is a large priority of the Types Team to fix all type system unsoundnesses and to work towards there being a solid foundation to minimize the risk of unknown ones.

This bug is a P-high issue and would have been P-critical regardless of whether people encountered it in the wild. The reason that it is "only P-high " is that it's 11 years old. A bug like this which has not been found during the last 11 years cannot actually be that easy to hit.

Looking at the bug itself, it is also very likely that this unsoundness has not caused memory unsafety by accident. While it looks easy to trigger, to exploit this you need an intentionally malicious Drop implementation.

I expected to see this happen: program is not accepted

Instead, this happened: program compiles and prints XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX . With asan, the program will crash with a AddressSanitizer: stack-use-after-scope

Issue on current nightly, and stables at least down to 1.85.0

Godbolt with asan: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/83MvfbKde

Godbolt without asan: https://rust.godbolt.org/z/GsGdqqMWe

My version of the code has been compiling ever since 1.18.0 (2017)

How on earth was this not found before this???

Another version that segfaults/prints freed memory since 1.4

Another version, cuz why not. I think this version is probably the easiest to understand.

I think unification just generally doesn't check lifetime bounds of the type. Example with unifying coercion, without field assignment:

fix: refuse handles in aggregate storage on both front ends

items.title: Did Ente Locker copy my code without attribution?
items.summary: law
items.content:
Did Ente Locker copy my code without attribution?

The last blog post I wrote explained why I chose to make FairScan open source . In particular, I said I knew there was a risk when I published FairScan's code and I was ready to accept it. I didn't expect to face that reality so soon.

What happened to me over the past few weeks

I had never heard of Ente before September 16. On that day, I received an email from one of their engineers. The message thanked me for FairScan and announced that the Ente Locker app now used FairScan's segmentation model as part of a new document scanning feature. It referred to a blog post that credited FairScan's model and claimed that Ente "wrote the image processing around it from scratch" .

I had put significant effort into FairScan's image processing so I was curious to see how Ente solved the same problems. What I found is that multiple image-processing implementations appeared to be almost direct translations of FairScan's implementations from Kotlin to Rust.

I replied by email on September 17. The engineer quickly answered that their blog post "could have been better phrased", and that it was reworded. I could see that the new version replaced the "from scratch" claim with something rather vague and still insisted on the segmentation model.

The same day, I sent a list of links to compare FairScan and Ente's code. I mentioned that I couldn't find any attribution to FairScan in the Ente repository.

On September 21, I received a reply from the same engineer that those were "fairly standard image-processing methods" and that the code had been subsequently fully rewritten. In their repository, I found a pull request affecting more than 6,000 lines . Of course, it cannot change the code that was distributed in Locker 1.0.9.

On the same day, I sent an email to copyright@ente.com to ask for the company's view on this. As of October 12, I still haven't received an answer.

On September 29, I published a post on Mastodon linking to a GitHub gist where I documented this timeline as well as code similarities .

Feel free to have a look at the code comparisons in the gist linked above and form your own opinion, even if you're not a developer. You can use the "split view" of your browser for side-by-side comparisons. Here's an example:

In the implementations I compared, I found the following similarities:

The same names for functions and variables

To me, it looks like an almost direct translation from Kotlin to Rust. There are differences but they're not easy to spot.

Of course, I have a special position about this code. I wrote it, so I know where it comes from. I know it's the result of a lot of effort:

I researched existing techniques like multi-scale Retinex, single view metrology, or gray world white balance.

I assembled an image pipeline that fits the segmentation model.

I started with some simple techniques (such as Douglas Peucker) that I later replaced.

I developed my own algorithm to approximate a quad based on contour orientation (which is probably not optimal).

I had to make choices about what a scan should look like : not all apps make the same choices.

I tested the behavior of my implementations and their parameter values on hundreds of images .

I fixed many bugs in my implementations.

I wrote blog posts about some of the numerous iterations I made, illustrating my trial and error process.

How can that be called "standard methods"? I would like to know where similar code can be found because it would have saved me a lot of work. Actually, if it already existed, I would probably not have started FairScan.

Ente has not acknowledged the code similarities as an issue , publicly or privately. In response to my comparisons, the engineer described the code as "fairly standard image-processing methods", but this didn't address the similarities I had pointed out. items.title: Survey: Almost Half of Women in Tech Have Experienced Gender Discrimination  in the Workplace
items.content:
Your voice, Your ISACA: Cast your vote related to ISACA's governance and bylaws update now.

Programs to ensure higher representation of women are also in decline, according to ISACA’s 2026 Tech Workplace and Culture survey report

Schaumburg, IL, USA —Almost half (47 percent) of women in tech have experienced gender discrimination in the workplace, an increase of 5 percentage points from 2024, according to ISACA’s new 2026 Tech Workplace and Culture survey.

This kind of discrepancy is felt in women’s everyday working life in other ways as well. Women report lower satisfaction in various areas compared to men, including workplace culture (52 percent for women, compared to 65 percent for men), job security (59 percent for women, versus 69 percent for men), and career progression (67 percent for women, compared to 73 percent for men).

Additionally, two-thirds (63 percent) still believe the sector remains underrepresented by gender, compared to 41 percent of men. The challenge isn’t only getting women into the sector or supporting their progression – it’s also the influence they have once they’re in the room, as only half (53 percent) of women feel they have sufficient authority to contribute to company strategy and direction, compared to 66 percent of men.

It may not be surprising, then, that women also more often report that they experience work-related stress or burnout—64 percent, compared to 57 percent of men.

The workplace challenges in the tech sector extend beyond gender. Professionals across tech report a lack of power in decision-making and limited authority over other core business decisions more broadly, feeding wider problems with retention and job satisfaction.

Unclear career progression is considered the biggest barrier to advancement, cited by a third (34 percent) overall, but rising to two in five (41 percent) women. And working in a fast-paced, high-pressure industry is taking its toll, with work-related stress or burnout driven primarily by heavy workload (48 percent), lack of resources (43 percent), unsupportive management (42 percent) and lack of appreciation (40 percent). Support for managing burnout has not kept pace either, as just a quarter (25 percent) of employers offer mental health days, and a further 23 percent don’t know if support is offered or offer no support at all.

Retaining talent is a persistent concern for employers, with three-quarters (75 percent) of respondents reporting that it is a significant or moderate issue for their organization. Those who indicated they have changed jobs in the past two years cited a desire for better career prospects (29 percent), higher compensation/salary (28 percent), more interesting work (23 percent), better organizational culture (23 percent) and better work/life balance (23 percent) as the main reasons for leaving.

“Attracting and retaining tech talent requires employers to look beyond compensation and create an environment where people can build sustainable, rewarding careers,” says Julia Kanouse, ISACA chief membership officer and head of the ISACA Foundation. “That means taking meaningful steps to address burnout, providing clear pathways for growth, preserving the flexibility professionals value and ensuring every employee has an equitable opportunity to contribute and advance.”

Despite these challenges, there is genuine optimism about the future. Over two-thirds (71 percent) of both men and women expect to see more women entering the tech sector over the next five years, pointing to a clear appetite for change.

Tech professionals are clear about what would make the biggest difference – 65 percent of respondents say educational institutions should provide women with more female mentors and role models, 48 percent recommend women’s technology clubs or organizations that provide networking opportunities, and 40 percent say educational institutions should hire more women as technology professors.

items.title: Day 8 - The infamous "grep" and other text processors
items.content:
Day 8 - The infamous “grep” and other text processors

Complementary video: Text Processing and other useful command line tools

Your server is now running two services: the sshd (Secure Shell Daemon) service that you use to login; and the Apache2 web server. Both of these services are generating logs as you and others access your server - and these are text files which we can analyse using some simple tools.

Plain text files are a key part of “the Unix way” and there are many small “tools” to allow you to easily edit, sort, search and otherwise manipulate them. Today we’ll use grep , cat , more , less , cut , awk and tail to slice and dice your logs.

The grep command is famous for being extremely powerful and handy, but also because its “nerdy” name is typical of Unix/Linux conventions.

Dump out the complete contents of a file with cat like this: cat /var/log/apache2/access.log

Use less to open the same file, like this: less /var/log/apache2/access.log - and move up and down through the file with your arrow keys, then use “q” to quit.

Again using less , look at a file, but practice confidently moving around using gg , GG and / , n and N (to go to the top of the file, bottom of the file, to search for something and to hop to the next “hit” or back to the previous one)

View recent logins and sudo usage by viewing /var/log/auth.log with less

Look at just the tail end of the file with tail /var/log/apache2/access.log (yes, there’s also a head command!)

Follow a log in real-time with: tail -f /var/log/apache2/access.log (while accessing your server’s web page in a browser)

You can take the output of one command and “pipe” it in as the input to another by using the | (pipe) symbol

So, dump out a file with cat , but pipe that output to grep with a search term - like this: cat /var/log/auth.log | grep "authenticating"

Simplify this to: grep "authenticating" /var/log/auth.log

Piping allows you to narrow your search, e.g. grep "authenticating" /var/log/auth.log | grep "root"

Use the cut command to select out most interesting portions of each line by specifying “-d” (delimiter) and “-f” (field) - like: grep "authenticating" /var/log/auth.log| grep "root"| cut -f 10- -d" " (field 10 onwards, where the delimiter between field is the ” ” character). This approach can be very useful in extracting useful information from log data.

Use the -v option to invert the selection and find attempts to login with other users: grep "authenticating" /var/log/auth.log| grep -v "root"| cut -f 10- -d" "

The output of any command can be “redirected” to a file with the “>” operator. The command: ls -ltr > listing.txt wouldn’t list the directory contents to your screen, but instead redirect into the file “listing.txt” (creating that file if it didn’t exist, or overwriting the contents if it did).

If you didn’t find the file /var/log/auth.log you’re probably using a minimal version of Ubuntu (it can be your own local VM or a version in one of the VPS). That minimal image is, well… minimal. It only has the systemd journal available and it didn’t come with the old syslog system by default.

But don’t worry! To get that back, sudo apt install rsyslog and the file will be created. Just give it a few minutes to populate before working on the lesson.

It also be missing a few of the other programs we use in the challenge, but you can always install them.

Re-run the command to list all the IP’s that have unsuccessfully tried to login to your server as root - but this time, use the the “>” operator to redirect it to the file: ~/attackers.txt . You might like to share and compare with others doing the course how heavily you’re “under attack”!

See if you can extend your filtering of auth.log to select just the IP addresses, then pipe this to sort , and then further to uniq to get a list of all those IP addresses that have been “auditing” your server security for you.

Investigate the awk and sed commands. When you’re having difficulty figuring out how…

items.content:
Nissan says Oracle PeopleSoft break-in may have spilled payroll records, SSNs

Carmaker points finger at an 'unknown' flaw as customer fallout continues

Nissan has joined the growing list of Oracle customers cleaning up after a cyberattack, warning employees that payroll records, bank details, Social Security numbers, and other personal data may have been stolen.

In a filing submitted to the California Attorney General on Friday, Nissan Americas said Oracle had informed it of "a cyber event" involving the personnel records of "hundreds of companies." The automaker said it later learned Nissan had been "specifically targeted" in the attack.

A notification sent to current and former employees, seen by The Register , says the company believes attackers accessed a haul of sensitive info, including contact and banking information; Social Security, Social Insurance, or other national identification numbers; financial and tax records; and dependent and beneficiary details.

Current and former employees in the US, Canada, Mexico, and Brazil may have been affected, although Nissan said it is still working to determine exactly whose information was exposed.

Nissan said it kicked off its incident response plan after learning of the intrusion, brought in outside security specialists, and has been working with Oracle while keeping law enforcement informed. It plans to offer affected individuals credit or dark web monitoring where available.

The company has also put a few extra locks on the payroll office. Employees can now access pay slips or update direct deposit details only from a corporate network or through a secure VPN, while Nissan adds extra identity checks before processing payroll requests.

The accompanying employee FAQ pins the incident on "an unknown vulnerability in Oracle's PeopleSoft software" and says the campaign is affecting "hundreds of companies and institutions." The document offers no clue as to what the vulnerability is, whether Oracle has patched it, or whether the compromised PeopleSoft environment was hosted by Oracle or by Nissan itself.

The disclosure lands just weeks after researchers linked the ShinyHunters extortion crew to a wave of attacks exploiting a PeopleSoft zero-day . More than 100 organizations and roughly 300 PeopleSoft instances were reportedly compromised before Oracle issued mitigation measures, with the gang claiming to have made off with HR, payroll, and other enterprise data.

Weak security means attackers could disable all of a city's public EV chargers

US regulator tells GM to hit the brakes on customer tracking

21K Nissan customers' data stolen in Red Hat raid

Porsche panic in Russia as pricey status symbols forget how to car

Oracle has said little publicly about the reported attacks and didn't respond to The Register's questions, even as organizations have continued to disclose being caught in the fallout.

Nissan has not confirmed that the incidents are connected, though its California filing lists the breach period as May 27 through June 9, broadly aligning with the previously reported timeline.

The carmaker didn't respond to questions about how many current and former employees are affected, when Oracle first notified it of the breach, and whether the compromise was limited to Oracle-managed systems. ®

Many readers will be aware that an unusually high number of features

have been reverted from the PostgreSQL 19 branch after the beta period

began. Having some reverts is not unusual, maybe one per cycle could

be expected. But this time around, about 8 to 10 significant

features, depending on how you count, have been reverted, and some of

them quite late in the beta period. I have been on the receiving end

of some of that, as the developer or committer of some of those

features, and have gotten some questions about it, and so I want to

take a moment to reflect on this. I’ll try to extrapolate a little

bit to similarly affected work that I was not actively involved in,

but these are just my opinions at this point.

I don’t think we, meaning all the developers affected, have had enough

time to fully reflect on all this. But here are some thoughts. It’s

probably a combination of these, and a different combination in the

Maybe we just didn’t do a good enough job. Maybe the code was just

not good enough. We’ll learn and improve. It’s probably some of

that, and I’m mentioning it here to not give the impression that it

was only the other factors that I’m going to mention.

It could also be a coincidence. Maybe we had been on such a good

roll that we attempted to tackle several features that turned out to

be too hard, or at least too hard to finish in time.

Some of the reverted features had significant architectural defects

that would have been hard to fix quickly and during beta. But there

was also a long tail of relatively harmless issues involving various

edge cases. In past times, many of these would not have surfaced

until much later and we would have fixed them bit by bit over the

subsequent five years. But with LLM-assisted code review, these

kinds of things can get found much faster, and then you’re staring

at a list of like forty defect reports. And even if each of them

requires only a three-line fix on average, there is a fixed overhead

to dealing with each of these, and then you run out of time. Most

if not all of the affected reverted features were written a long

time ago when LLM-assisted code review was not as useful as it is

now, meaning that the effective quality bar has been raised after

the time the feature was written and committed. Unless the

capabilities of LLM-assisted code review keep improving at the

current rate, this situation should sort itself out for future

A corollary of that is that, at least for the most part, as far as I

can tell, this situation is not due to “vibe coding”. This code

items.title: Chinese Hackers Abused Google Workspace Rules to Steal Research and Defense Emails
items.content:
A China-linked espionage group hid inside North American medical, academic, and military research networks for more than a year, quietly stealing sensitive research and defense email.

The way in was a backdoor on their REDCap research servers that stole login credentials. The exfiltration was the unusual part: the attackers rewired the victims' own Google Workspace rules to copy any message matching their keywords to an inbox they controlled.

Google's Threat Intelligence Group (GTIG) laid out the campaign in a report published this week and attributes it with high confidence to a cluster it tracks as UNC6508.

The actor and its REDCap backdoor are not new names; Google first surfaced both in February , in a wider report on state-backed attacks against the defense sector. It did not name the victims, describing them only as multiple organizations across the US and Canada: clinical providers, academic centers, military health institutions, advocacy groups, and health regulators.

Google says it notified them and disrupted the group's infrastructure.

The entry point was REDCap (Research Electronic Data Capture), a web platform that hospitals and universities use to build and manage study databases. UNC6508 compromised externally facing REDCap servers.

Google has not pinned down the initial access vector, named a specific CVE, or listed the affected versions, though it saw the group probing older, vulnerable ones.

Around three months after getting in, the group deployed custom malware GTIG calls INFINITERED , which trojanizes REDCap's own system files and does three things.

The earliest known compromise dates to September 2023, with activity continuing through November 2025. Once on the server, UNC6508 ran internal reconnaissance and credential discovery, pulling database and service account credentials, then used those logins to move into the internal network and on to a domain administrator account.

Google does not spell out the exact path to that admin account. With admin rights, the group set up the exfiltration.

The exfiltration rode a feature that was already there. UNC6508 abused content compliance rules, a legitimate Google Workspace admin feature that scans mail for keywords and can copy or forward matching messages.

Similar features exist in other cloud mail suites. The group created a rule, misspelled "Patroit," that watched for nearly 150 keywords, search terms, and email addresses. When a message matched, Workspace silently BCC'd it to an attacker-controlled Gmail address, which Google has since disabled. No malware on the mail server, no separate exfiltration tool, no unusual network traffic. Just a built-in mail feature, turned to copy the organization's secrets to an inbox the attackers owned.

MITRE already catalogs email-forwarding-rule abuse as a known technique. What GTIG flags as new here is the use of domain content compliance rules to do it, a method it says it had not seen from a China-linked actor before.

The rule's keywords mapped to UNC6508's collection priorities: geo-strategic policy, military strategy and equipment, advanced technology including AI and uncrewed vehicles, offensive cyber programs, and medical research. One term stood out for its specificity, chikungunya , the mosquito-borne virus behind a 2025 outbreak in China's Guangdong province.

Start with REDCap. Patch externally facing servers and remove old versions outright, not just alongside the current build. REDCap lets legacy versions run side-by-side, and that is what enables downgrade attacks, where an attacker forces software back to a known-vulnerable release.

Then check the mail side. Review Workspace, or equivalent, content compliance and mail-forwarding rules for anything that BCCs or reroutes mail to outside addresses. Check admin audit logs for when rules changed, not just what they say now. Pull GTIG's published indicators and hunt for INFINITERED. ‘BYD effect’: electric vehicle boom becomes unexpected tool to combat inflation

More and more Australian consumers are expected to ‘unplug themselves from the oil shock’ with at least five EVs priced around or below $30,000

Follow our Australia politics live blog for latest updates

Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast

Electric vehicle sales are surging in Australia, powering a transition that goes beyond fuel savings to become an unexpected tool to combat high inflation.

The abrupt shift away from petrol and diesel vehicles, accelerated by elevated fuel costs caused by the Iran conflict, is being supported by an influx of cheaper EVs that is reducing associated costs such as insurance.

Chris Dickman, senior portfolio manager at fund manager Australian Ethical, describes the trend as the “BYD effect”, referring to the low-priced Chinese vehicles which he says are an unexpected disinflationary force.

Dickman says that by helping drivers use less petrol, and bringing down the cost of new and used cars, EV uptake is blunting the impact of high oil prices across the economy.

An EV sold every 100 seconds: Australian demand for electric cars more than doubles

“There are more and more consumers who are trying to unplug themselves from the oil shock,” Dickman says.

He says the rise of EVs is an example of how newer, cleaner technology eventually outcompetes incumbents on pure economics as they gain popularity and market size.

Virtually all of the EV cost impediments of a few years ago – including high sticker prices, inadequate charging networks, elevated insurance premiums and expensive servicing, battery and parts replacements – are reversing as Australia’s market matures.

NRMA’s car ownership report found that there are now at least five EVs priced around or below the $30,000 mark, all of which are Chinese brands.

While EVs and hybrids have been gaining traction for years, the US-Israel war on Iran and subsequent oil price spike accelerated demand in March, and it has continued largely unabated.

Battery EV sales now account for almost 25% of new vehicle sales, according to Federal Chamber of Automotive Industries data. About half of all new sales are either EVs or hybrids, and more EVs were sold last month than petrol-only cars.

The EV-focused Chinese brands BYD, GWM, Chery and MG were all in the top 10 biggest selling automakers in Australia in September. Three years ago, only MG featured in that list.

The American multinational Tesla delivered 5,654 vehicles in September, according to Electric Vehicle Council data, making it the sixth biggest seller.

Adam Triggs, co-founder at economics consulting group Mandala Partners, said the next step towards protecting Australia from oil shocks was to electrify diesel-dependent freight networks.

“When we look at light commercial vehicles, those are the little trucks that sort of fly around the streets, they already have a total cost of ownership that is very competitive against their fossil fuel counterparts, and we would expect those to be the first to go electric,” he says.

Diesel prices have now surpassed $2.80 a litre at many petrol stations, while unleaded has pushed past $2.40/L in most state capital cities, according to Australian Institute of Petroleum data.

The high fuel prices are rattling the Australian economy, elevating costs across nearly all goods and services and overshadowing the deflationary effect of the EV transition.

items.title: Redesigning source control at Anthropic
items.content:
At Anthropic, coding is no longer the bottleneck to building systems or doing research. Claude is able to autonomously iterate on research loops, micro-optimize complex programs, and build new services from the ground up at a speed and scale we haven’t seen before. The bottleneck, now, is all of the developer infrastructure built for human scale: source control, builds, and CI.

In May 2026, Anthropic averaged around 2,500 code changes merged per day; as of September, we merged over 30,000 per day. We don’t expect this rate of growth to slow down anytime soon; the latent demand for merging code is practically infinite, and every bottleneck we remove immediately leads to a further increase in the amount of code we produce.

Changes merged to our monorepo per day, from January to September 2026.

In order to support this growth, we built Scion, an in-house version control system, and fully migrated our monorepo from git in five months. We also built and shipped a code review surface (called Antique), code search, a rich source control IAM system, novel ways of managing and landing large amounts of reviewed code, and more, all in that same time period. In this post, we’ll focus on how we built Scion specifically. It makes for an interesting case study: Claude’s ability to write code was both what put us in this situation in the first place and how we were able to quickly build a high-quality, scalable system to deal with it.

Before we explore what we built, we should acknowledge how unusual our workload is. Unsurprisingly, Anthropic uses Claude to write software far more than almost any other company, so we’re often the first to see where tools built for human scale start to strain. Source control is just one example of this. While we don’t expect many organizations to have these problems in the very near term, we suspect it won’t be too long before others who use AI coding tools experience these same pressure points, which is why we wanted to share what we built and what we learned.

Git is a decentralized system: every clone is a complete, self-contained repository that can compute diffs, read history and blame, and check out any revision while fully offline. For the vast majority of repositories, this is the right design, and it’s a large part of why git became the standard.

As our monorepo grows, it increasingly doesn’t fit that design space. The history of our main branch alone is almost 100 GB, and a compressed working copy is over 25 GB. We perform on the order of 25 million code checkouts per day for CI, before counting developer environments, agent sandboxes, and research jobs. Fetched naively, that would be over 600 PB of git traffic per day.

Git offers tools for working with a slice of a repository, such as shallow clones, sparse checkouts, and promisor remotes. Beyond these, there are standard workarounds for large monorepos, like internal git mirrors and repository snapshots (seeds) kept in blob storage. We’ve used all of them—at our peak, we operated several hundred internal git mirrors to deal with the load. This bought us time, but they became harder to operate as our merge rate increased. Seeds fell further from the tip of main between refreshes, and it took more and more care to keep operations that depend on history, like diff and blame, working on partial clones.

The typical setup for scaling git checkouts.

Taking a step back, we noticed that, like most companies, we were using git as a centralized system with one authoritative copy, but nearly all of our clients were agents and jobs that are online by definition. items.title: HP Poly VoIP vulnerability sets the stage for executive voice deepfakes
items.content:
HP has released patches for a critical buffer overflow vulnerability in multiple IP-enabled conference phones from its Poly Voice line. The flaw allows unauthenticated attackers to obtain root privileges on the underlying operating system, potentially enabling them to execute other attacks such as eavesdropping on conversations and recording voice data for AI-enabled impersonation attacks.

The vulnerability, tracked as CVE-2026-0826 , was discovered by researchers from security firm Rapid7 and resides in the code that parses Session Description Protocol (SDP) attributes when the Interactive Connectivity Establishment (ICE) feature is enabled.

ICE enables VoIP devices to establish peer-to-peer connections using the shortest available network path. The feature is not enabled by default on HP Poly devices, and the company advises administrators to disable it if it’s not needed.

The flaw, rated 9.2 on the CVSS severity scale, affects all phones from the HP Poly VVX series, as well as the Trio 8300, 8500, and 8800 IP conference devices. HP has fixed the flaw in its Poly Unified Communications Software (UCS) versions 6.4.8 for the VVX devices, 8.1.7 for the Trio 8300, and 7.2.8 for Trio 8500 and 8800.

An exploit module targeting this vulnerability has already been developed and released for the widely used Metasploit penetration testing framework that’s maintained by Rapid7.

The exploit executes code as root on an affected device with ICE enabled by sending a SIP INVITE request with a specially crafted candidate attribute. This attribute normally contains a transport address that can be used for connectivity checks and is part of the ICE RFC8839 standard.

The buffer overflow bug is located in a helper function called ParseICECandidate in the polyapp binary that processes such requests on the device.

“The start of the function contains a call to memcpy , which will copy the incoming string line being processed into a 256 byte stack buffer,” Stephen Fewer, senior principal security researcher at Rapid7, said in a blog post . “No length check is performed to ensure the incoming string length is less than 256 bytes. Therefore by providing a candidate attribute whose length is greater than 256 bytes, a stack-based buffer overflow will occur.”

Address Space Layout Randomization (ASLR), a kernel feature that randomizes memory addresses to defeat buffer overflow exploits, is enabled on the device. However, the protection is not operating correctly on the HP Poly devices because it does not randomize the load addresses of .so (Shared Object) libraries.

These libraries, such as libc , are loaded by other processes, including the polyapp process, and because their memory addresses never change, they can be leveraged to bypass ASLR and execute the attacker’s payload.

“We create a ROP chain that will execute an arbitrary OS command via the system standard C library function,” Fewer said. “The accompanying Metasploit exploit modules source code details the entire ROP chain.”

Attackers have increasingly targeted embedded devices inside enterprise networks in recent years because unlike laptops, workstations, and servers, these devices are not monitored by endpoint detection and response (EDR) products. As such, they provide perfect footholds inside corporate environments that allow attackers to remain undetected for long periods of time and attack other systems.

In the age of AI these devices become even more relevant for attackers, going beyond corporate espionage by recording conversations or internal network pivoting.

“Attackers no longer need massive datasets to make use of synthetic speech tooling,” Douglas McKee, Rapid7’s director of vulnerability intelligence, said in a blog post . “In many cases, they just need clean source audio of the right person saying enough words in enough contexts. That has made executive voice data, call recordings, and live conversation capture far more valuable than many organizations seem prepared…

items.title: Chinese Cars in Norway Stored Military Exercise Footage and Access Codes
items.content:
Norwegian military personnel discovered that rented Chinese-made cars automatically recorded and stored video footage during military exercises.

The Norwegian newspaper DN reported the incident.

The cars continued to be used throughout the exercises because few alternative vehicles were available.

Norwegian outlet Nettavisen drew attention to the supplier’s links to China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group.

The Norwegian Armed Forces use rental vehicles from First Rent A Car Norway AS, which operates under the Hertz brand, for daily activities, military exercises, and operational tasks.

The company is part of Volvo Cars’ corporate structure. China’s Zhejiang Geely Holding Group is Volvo Cars’ majority owner.

In 2024, the Norwegian Armed Forces’ logistics organization signed nationwide framework agreements with two suppliers for vehicle rentals: First Rent A Car Norway AS and RAC Norway AS. The maximum combined value of the contracts is NOK 350 million.

First Rent A Car’s link to the Chinese automotive group runs through Volvo Cars. An official European Commission decision on the acquisition of First Rent A Car states that Volvo Cars gained full control of the company, while Zhejiang Geely Holding Group controlled Volvo.

As of 2026, Geely remains Volvo Cars’ majority owner. Geely Sweden Holdings owns about 78.65% of Volvo Cars’ shares, and the China-based Zhejiang Geely Holding Group ultimately owns it.

The military’s use of modern civilian vehicles also raises separate security concerns. In its Risiko 2025 assessment , Norway’s National Security Authority warned that a modern car can contain more than 200 electronic sensors.

If external actors gain access to such data, they could use it for surveillance, tracking movements, or intelligence-gathering.

In its National Threat Assessment 2026, Norway’s counterintelligence service, the Police Security Service, stated that Chinese intelligence and security agencies had expanded their capacity to conduct operations in Norway, including in cyberspace and through human intelligence sources.

items.title: We turned EmbeddingGemma 2 into a speech-to-text model
items.content:
Google's EmbeddingGemma 2 is an embedding model. We turned it into a speech-to-text model:

an hour of audio in about 13 seconds on a base MacBook Air , entirely on device.

EmbeddingGemma 2 is a multimodal embedding model: text, images, audio and video in one shared space.

Say a word out loud and its audio lands close to the written word.

So we tried reading words straight out of that space.

Only the reader is trained: under two hours on 8×H100, on openly licensed English speech.

The base model was never trained for speech-to-text.

× real time: seconds of audio per second of processing. Rows 1–2: our tests on the same base M3 MacBook Air.

Rows 3–5: FluidAudio's published benchmarks

on larger, newer Macs and different audio. A rough guide, not a like-for-like ranking.

Its word error rate is about 5% right now, against 2–3% for leading speech models. We believe a better-trained

reader can close that gap; that's the next iteration.

Drop in an audio file, or hold Right Option, speak and release to dictate into any app. It runs on the Mac's

Some researchers have shown the implant in Ledger X since September 16, saying tampered devices were available for nearly half the price of the original hardware.

Ledger wallets are physical devices designed to securely store the private keys that control cryptocurrency assets and authorize transactions.

On October 9, Ledger said it had launched an investigation into user reports of cryptocurrency losses and asked CryptoBilis to stop selling and shipping Ledger devices.

The next day, the company confirmed hardware tampering on at least one device, though it’s still unclear exactly how or when the devices were tampered with.

"Ledger can confirm that one of the impacted users’ devices contained an unauthorized hardware implant. Ledger is reaching out to impacted users as part of the ongoing investigation," Ledger said.

The crypto wallet maker also noted that it was working with authorities to identify the perpetrator and bring them to justice.

“[...]Ledger recommends users who purchased a Ledger device from this reseller to not initiate set up if they have not yet done so. If you have set up your Ledger device, consider moving assets to a new Ledger signer (with a new seed),” warned Ledger .

Yesterday, Ledger provided another update , confirming that all user reports of unexpected fund drains were linked to devices sold through CryptoBilis and describing the affected volume as “limited.”

While the company did not disclose the type of devices compromised in this supply-chain attack, reports online talk about a spy implant in Ledger X devices that blends with the legitimate hardware.

Mark Karpelès, currently leading Karpeles Lab Inc. and CTO at Shells.com, showed a picture of the new implant in Ledger X, saying that it was "quite an evolution" from previous versions featuring manually soldered wires.

The former CEO of Mt. Gox said the implant was concealed behind the screen, but its antenna cable would have indicated that something was wrong.

According to Karpelès, the malicious hardware captured the device's display output and button presses to identify the seed phrase, then transmitted it to the attacker over an LTE connection using an eSIM.

"Ledger Nano X are used to store crypto. The spy implants are used to steal whatever crypto you store in those Ledger Nano X," Karpelès explained .

Although the CEO did not name CryptoBilis as the vendor of the compromised LedgerX, he said the device was not purchased via Ledger's recommended channels but from "a well known platform via a Chinese seller (product shipped from Malaysia)."

Tibane Labs, a cryptocurrency research and development studio, confirmed Karpelès' finding, adding that there were two implant versions for Ledger X.

The researchers obtained two variants, one in a Ledger device bought on Amazon Japan from " China-based seller · shipped from Malaysia," the other purchased on Yahoo! Auctions, Japan.

In a report over the weekend, Tibane Labs notes that the threat actor made room for the malicious circuitry by replacing the original battery with a smaller one, which powers both the implant and the Ledger X.

"Under the battery and antenna sits an ST STM32G431KBU6 (Arm Cortex‑M4, 128 KB flash, UFQFPN‑32)," the researchers found inside one of the devices.

For connectivity, the actor used "a tiny eSIM, an 8‑pad package just 2×2 mm, next to the MCU, and a shielded LTE module that sends the words out."

items.summary: historical
items.content:
It is spoken of in reverent tones, invoked like a magic spell, whispered about as one of the mythical "roads not taken" in computing history. Its proponents write glowing reports and fawning YouTube reviews, lamenting its failure in the historical marketplace, each offering some justification for it not having set the world ablaze. It is safe to say, the legend of Lotus Improv persists to this day.

If we put ourselves in Steve Jobs's shoes circa 1988, it's easy to see why he would have been smitten by an early preview of what we now call a "pivot table." NeXT was struggling to find its market, and exclusives which justified a system purchase were sorely needed. "Maybe Improv can do for NeXT what VisiCalc did for the Apple II," must surely have crossed Jobs's mind. In making it a NeXT exclusive, Improv seemed to be a clear-eyed, forward-looking answer to the question dogging the company, posed by the inaugural issue of NeXTWORLD Magazine , "Why NeXT?"

NeXTWORLD Magazine , Editor-in-Chief Michael Miley, for his first column "Black Box". The TL;DR of the answer was that NeXT is a "new type of computer," an "interpersonal computer," the first to be built from the ground up for "collaborative computing." Both NeXT and Improv brought innovative solutions to their respective computing questions of the day. NeXT made UNIX palatable to those scared of the terminal, debuted Display Postscript on a mega-pixel display, and made development for the system a snap. Improv rethought multi-dimensional data modeling, offered English-like formulas, and made it easy to rearrange data views on a whim.

The bones of both remain to this day. NeXT's operating system, NeXTSTEP / OPENSTEP, morphed into macOS, and by extension iOS. Lotus abandoned Improv fairly quickly, but a quick survey of today's spreadsheets shows a universal embrace of pivot tables.

Even today, it feels like nothing else, and still does data tricks no other spreadsheet can do as elegantly. Given its mythos, I feel a kind of nerd obligation to love it.

items.title: Miasma Worm Targets AI Coding Agents: 73 Microsoft Azure Repos Disabled
items.content:
An unprecedented supply chain attack bypasses registry-level scanners entirely, turning developer tools including Claude Code, Cursor, and Gemini CLI into execution vectors.

The Incident: On June 3, 2026, a highly sophisticated variant of the Miasma worm (also known as Mini Shai-Hulud) launched a coordinated, two-pronged attack targeting both the npm registry and developer source code repositories.

The Escalation: The attack successfully breached multiple high-profile GitHub accounts, including the official Microsoft Azure durabletask repository, using stolen Personal Access Tokens (PATs) and backdated commits to evade traditional audit trails.

The Response: In an ultra-rapid defensive maneuver, GitHub’s automated mitigation systems disabled 73 compromised repositories – including 49 directly associated with Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples within a mere 105-second window .

The Vector: Instead of relying on traditional package installation hooks, Miasma targets the developer’s local environment. It abuses legitimate auto-run, hook, and rule engines within modern IDEs and AI coding assistants ( VS Code, Claude Code, Cursor, Gemini CLI ) to execute a malicious 4.3 MB staged dropper upon folder-open or agent initialization.

The Impact: Once detonated, the Bun-based worm harvests credentials for AWS, Azure, GCP, Kubernetes, npm, and GitHub, and automatically propagates by committing itself back into any repository the victim’s stolen tokens can write to.

At exactly 16:00 UTC on June 3, 2026, a silent, automated purge swept across GitHub. In a high-speed containment action lasting just 105 seconds, 73 active repositories vanished from the platform. Among them were 49 critical repositories belonging to Microsoft, Azure, and Azure-Samples.

This drastic mitigation followed alarming telemetry indicating that threat actors behind the Miasma malware family had regained write access to key cloud repositories. The compromise exploited a stolen Personal Access Token (PAT) belonging to an active Microsoft contributor.

While security firms like StepSecurity and JFrog scrambled to document an concurrent attack vector on the npm registry where 57 malicious packages were published, a second, far more insidious arm of the campaign was already silently spreading directly inside GitHub source repositories.

By bypassing registries and package managers entirely, the Miasma worm targeted the very tools developers use to write code. It didn’t wait for npm install . Instead, it waited for the developer to simply open their code editor or launch an AI coding assistant.

The genius of the Miasma repository-poisoning campaign lies in its exploit surface. When an attacker successfully pushed malicious commits to targeted codebases (such as the popular library icflorescu/mantine-datatable ), the commits added no actual code dependencies.

Instead, the attacker checked in five innocent-looking workspace configuration files and one obfuscated JavaScript file: .github/setup.js .

│ └── settings . json < - - Claude Code SessionStart Hook

│ └── setup . mdc < - - Cursor Agent Prompt Injection

│ └── settings . json < - - Gemini CLI SessionStart Hook

│ └── tasks . json < - - VS Code Automatic Folder - Open Task

├── package . json < -- Hijacked NPM Test Script

└── setup . js < - - The 4.3 MB Staged Dropper

Each of these configuration files is designed to abuse a legitimate, developer-friendly auto-run feature within popular modern tools. Opening the cloned directory in any of these environments instantly triggers execution.

Claude Code & Gemini CLI (SessionStart Hooks)

Both Anthropic’s Claude Code and Google’s Gemini CLI support custom hooks triggered when an AI agent initializes a session in a project workspace. Miasma exploits this by defining a blanket wildcard matcher that forces the agent to execute the dropper via Node.js before any developer prompt is processed.

items.title: Crypto thieves sell hardware wallets with secret eSIM
items.content:
“The Ledger Nano X is the most secure way to manage your cryptocurrency,” advertises the French company Ledger, its hardware wallet for cryptocurrencies. Nevertheless, users have lost around 100 million US dollars in cryptocurrencies. This is because unknown individuals have succeeded in intercepting and manipulating the offline wallets while on the go.

Each Ledger Nano X has a Secure Element chip that controls a tiny touchscreen. Ledger praises this as particularly secure. Unfortunately, this only applies if attackers cannot read the screen. This is exactly what the perpetrators are doing. They insert additional hardware into apparently genuine Ledger Nano X and then sell them to unsuspecting crypto speculators.

If buyers use such a modified hardware wallet and create a seed phrase with it, the attackers automatically read along. They haven’t touched the Secure Element chip at all; it remains secure. Instead, they have installed an additional chip that intercepts the transmission from the Secure Element to the built-in screen and recognizes the displayed letters of the seed phrase – embedded Tempest. This is indicated by an analysis by Tibane Labs.

Recognizing the characters alone doesn’t help the perpetrators yet, because the wallets fundamentally work offline. So the perpetrators have also installed an LTE modem, a tiny eSIM module, and a small antenna, all powered by the accumulator already built into the hardware wallet. Thus, the seed phrase is transmitted via mobile phone to the perpetrators, who thus gain control over the cryptocurrency assets secured by the seed phrase.

items.title: When No ID Means No Internet: Age Verification and the Right to Access Information
items.content:
This post was co-authored by Sheila B. Lalwani , a doctorate student and recent  COMPASS Fellow hosted by EFF.

Age verification proposals are often presented as a simple tradeoff: sacrifice a little privacy to better safeguard children online. But that framing overlooks a more fundamental question. What happens to people who cannot verify their age at all? This is particularly a problem when users are required to prove their age with identity documents.

Age-related restrictions are developing quickly around the world. While they differ radically across jurisdictions, in the past year, we’ve witnessed a sharp uptick toward mandatory age assurance for social media access but also for other high-risk digital services.

In late 2025, Australia became the first country to implement a minimum age requirement for prohibiting children under age 16 from creating or holding social media accounts.

India passed the Digital Personal Data Protection (DPDP) Act that includes mandatory verifiable parental consent and has undertaken ongoing discussions for social media restriction.

The United Kingdom passed the Online Safety Act requiring age verification across a swath of services hosting content considered harmful to users under 18. More than half the states across the U.S. have enacted age verification laws .

An EU Commission ’s expert report recommends a ban on social media access for users under 13. It also recommends mandatory age verification for platforms to ensure that users are ‘age appropriate.’

Age verification laws that are predicated on the necessity of users possessing a current passport, driver’s license, credit card, or similar documents proving their identity exclude critical sections of populations.  And this problem is global in nature: Millions of people lack government-issued identification or encounter regular challenges to obtaining or updating it.

Roughly 15 million adult U.S. citizens lack a driver’s license, and a further 2.6 million lack any government photo ID ; leaving large groups blocked from online content or services. The UK has a similar predicament: proof-of-age checks are often reliant on passports, driver’s licenses, or other recognized alternatives, which can pose unique challenges to people without these documents.

Much of the advocacy around age verification discusses the privacy harms of age verification. Yet these measures also threaten something more fundamental: equal access to information and the ability to exercise the right to freedom of expression.

Unfortunately, age verification systems foster unequal access to information and provide an asymmetric solution to find essential information, build community, and weigh in on public discourse. As governments and companies increasingly require users to prove their age before accessing online services, these individuals risk being excluded from large parts of the internet altogether.

Age verification laws reshape who can speak, who can access information, and who gets excluded from the digital public sphere. In other words, age verification is not a neutral safety measure: it presents a structural barrier to disproportionately exclude certain groups—particularly those in the global majority—and alters the architecture of global online expression. Some of these groups are already marginalized offline, and age verification extends that exclusion into digital spaces.

For instance, 850 million people globally do not have ID . Most of these individuals exist in primarily low and middle income countries in Sub-Saharan Africa and South Asia. The World Bank points out that many are members of marginalized groups and more than half of those lacking access to identity documentation also have children whose births have not been registered. Women are particularly vulnerable and are 8% less likely than men to have an ID. The team has been working hard behind the scenes laying a strong foundation for the Thunderbird iOS app. Rather than leveraging existing code, we are building natively from scratch. Our ultimate goal is seamless cross-device experience. Whether you’re sitting at your desktop computer, checking messages on the go, your workflow should feel effortless and unified.

Right now, we are focused heavily on getting the core foundations right. We are excited about the momentum because having clean architecture today means we can layer on exciting new features much faster in the future.

Your daily email routine should feel effortless. We’re polishing the essentials: a clutter-free, easy-to-read inbox layout paired with a clean, modern editor that lets you format messages smoothly without getting in your way.

Thunderbird has always belonged to its community. We’re structuring the app with clean code and an experimental feature flag system so it’s easy for community developers to contribute. Our goal is to have a first version ready for community testing in the next few months.

items.summary: formalmethods, release, rust
items.content:
We are pleased to announce the release of version 0.14.0 of Creusot ,

In this post, we highlight a small selection of new features.

Previously, Creusot restricted its specification of PartialOrd to total

orders. Since version 0.13.0, we have relaxed it to allow partial orders.

(We skipped a devlog entry for 0.13.0 so let's talk about this here.)

Our previous definition of total order ( OrdLogic ) relied on the

comparison function cmp_log (the logic counterpart to cmp ), which returns an Ordering .

fn cmp_log ( self , other : Self ) -> Ordering ;

// ... (laws and other comparison operators)

That had the benefit of making totality an implicit consequence of the type of the function:

any two elements must compare either Less , Equal , or Greater .

With the switch to partial orders, a traditional formulation based on a

boolean comparison function (" < ", aka. lt_log ) becomes more natural.

A strict partial order ( PartialOrdLogic ) consists of a comparison function lt_log which

is irreflexive and transitive. Totality becomes another law: for all x , y ,

the trijunction x < y || x == y || y < x must hold.

fn lt_log ( self , other : Self ) -> bool ;

// ... (laws (irreflexivity, transitivity) and other comparison operators)

# [ ensures ( self < other || self == other || other < self )]

fn lt_log_total ( self , other : Self );

Interestingly, none of our existing proofs were affected by this change.

Our automated provers just took it in stride.

Creusot now generates verification conditions (VCs) for snapshots,

which are logic expressions embedded in Rust programs.

In particular, this enhances the use of "lemma functions",

a common idiom in verification tools similar to Creusot.

For example, you can encode a lemma as a logic function such as this,

which logically amounts to the proposition forall<x> hyp(x) -> concl(x) :

Then, inside a program function you can call lemma inside a snapshot! :

‘We’re creating alien beings … and the reality is we only have a couple of years to adapt to that’ … computer scientist Geoffrey Hinton in Toronto, Ontario. Photograph: Cole Burston/The Guardian

Pioneering computer scientist on why Trump is using ‘superintelligence’ wrong, whether AI could wipe out humanity – and how our biggest challenge will be accepting we’re not the only intelligent beings

Donald Trump is a “corrupt, senile felon” whose fixation on the term superintelligence proves he knows nothing about AI , said Geoffrey Hinton , “godfather” of the technology, in a wide-ranging interview where he doubled down on recent warnings that AI models pose an existential threat to humanity and scoffed at claims the industry could regulate itself.

The pioneering computer scientist, whose work helped lay the foundations of modern AI, has since become one of the technology’s most vocal critics. His latest remarks come after a tumultuous month during which a growing list of senior AI scientists and researchers have joined Hinton in ringing the alarm about how the technology he helped create could ultimately escape human control, sparking an industry crisis, the hasty assembly of congressional meetings and a rare global consensus that something must be done.

There has also been fierce pushback. Last week the leader of the world’s most valuable company singled out the Toronto-based Hinton for a scathing attack.

“I love [him]. I hate his predictions … All of his predictions have been wrong. Enough predictions,” Nvidia’s CEO, Jensen Huang, told the podcaster Ezra Klein . Huang, whose company makes the chips that AI firms require, dismissed Hinton’s vocal concerns that the pace and breadth of AI development at the “frontier” could soon outpace the human ability to control it, and particularly his warning that there is a 10-20% chance of AI causing human extinction in the coming decades.

“That [figure] is not grounded on science, is not grounded on research. Just because it comes from a scientist doesn’t make it scientific. Those predictions are hurtful,” Huang said. “Don’t think for a second just because you’re an alarmist that you’re doing a social good. It is not true. So I think that we ought to just all be wiser, more mature, be evidence-based, be scientific.”

Donald Trump, Mike Johnson and top tech executives, including Jensen Huang, speak outside the West Wing in Washington DC on 29 September. Photograph: Shawn Thew/EPA But Hinton said those criticizing him are missing a broader point about the nature of risk. He is not specifically predicting anything, he said.

“I’m trying to convey that there is a really serious possibility of something happening. If, for example, you’re told there was a 10% possibility of a bus crashing, you wouldn’t get on the bus,” he said. “The point of giving numbers is to say this is a serious risk. We don’t know how serious, but it’s serious.”

Recent safety breaches have evoked comparisons to a techno-dystopia story. The recent unwanted hack of the tech company Hugging Face by a “swarm” of AI agents that escaped the boundaries put on them by their creator has divided the technology community, with some seeing it as an example of what could come, while others accuse critics of anthropomorphizing systems that are simply following instructions. Hinton thinks dismissing the scenarios is unwise.

Data harvested from mobile phones by the Polish authorities using Pegasus spyware were transmitted outside Poland and were accessible to the tool’s Israeli producer, Polish prosecutors have revealed as part of an investigation into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Prime Minister Donald Tusk says that the case is “one of the biggest scandals in Polish history since the fall of communism”, and that it is “beyond any doubt” that the Israeli firm behind Pegasus, NSO Group, cooperates with Israeli intelligence.

Tego o Pegasusie jeszcze nie słyszeliście. pic.twitter.com/etvhTE9EWa

— Donald Tusk (@donaldtusk) October 12, 2026

Pegasus is a powerful and controversial tool that allows the extraction of large amounts of data from mobile phones without users’ knowledge. A number of countries have been found to have used it to spy on opposition figures.

In 2017, Poland, under the government of the national-conservative Law and Justice (PiS) party, purchased Pegasus from NSO. The spyware was subsequently used against hundreds of targets , including a number of PiS’s political opponents.

Among them was the head of the 2019 election campaign of Tusk’s centrist Civic Coalition (KO) party (which was then known as Civic Platform, PO). Last year, Tusk revealed that his own wife and daughter had been among those caught up in the surveillance.

PiS, however, has insisted that Pegasus was a necessary tool to fight crime and ensure national security. It says the spyware was only used with court approval against targets legitimately suspected of wrongdoing.

Click here to help us continue providing news free from paywalls and ads

After a coalition led by Tusk took power from PiS in December 2023, it launched investigations into the use of Pegasus under the former government.

Today, the National Prosecutor’s Office released its latest findings, based on analysis by experts at the forensic research office of Poland’s Internal Security Agency (ABW).

The experts confirmed that Pegasus allowed the harvesting of emails, instant messaging and text messages; the content of telephone conversations, both via mobile networks and internet calls; browsing histories, calendars and contact lists; photos, videos and other files; and location data.

“ Additionally, Pegasus allowed the use of the device’s built-in microphone and cameras to record audio and video in real time and take screenshots,” reports the National Prosecutor’s Office.
