items.title: A slightly faster slimmer curl
items.summary: performance
items.content:
Back in August I mentioned the new curl performance tests we have running. I figured it could be apt to return to this topic just to mention some of the initial outcomes.

When the team gets a new set of charts, graphs and plots that visualize something, like performance, they offer an excellent opportunity for us to try to make them look better. This new setup is no exception.

The performance tests have only been running for just a little over two months but they have already made us improve curl performance in several areas. Of course, for most transfers these changes won’t make many visible differences to users. This is more in the vein that every little bit counts and that nothing should run slower than it has to.

This is a list of some improvements that are included in the curl 8.23.0 release, to be shipped tomorrow on October 14.

With a few different changes, the internal base64 encoding function is more than twice as fast, while base64 decoding is 40% faster.

Meaning percent encoding the octets that are not safe to use in URLs. The decoding function now runs more than twice as fast compare to before, while the encoding function is around four times as fast.

Converting a date provided in plain ASCII text, as is used in for example cookie headers, to the epoch – number of seconds since Jan 1st 1970, is now more than twice as fast as before. Mostly thanks to completely replaced functions for week day, month name and time zone name lookups.

Parsing a full URL to split it up into separate components as well as confirming its validity is a core component of curl, and libcurl exposes this functionality in its API.

In a test with several hundred different URLs, the new version executes 20-30% faster than before – with an improved ability to return precisely what the problem was when the URL is considered invalid.

For portability and now historical reasons, libcurl has its own printf() implementation. This ensures that it always works identically on all platforms but it also makes it our job to make sure it executes as fast as possible.

Most printf() calls now run slightly faster (5-15%) because it handles “chunks” instead of single byte-by-byte at a time.

We have a generic internal function in curl that converts a number provided in ascii to its binary version (for decimal, hexadecimal and octal). It handles 64 bit values, has overflow detection and supports a maximum. This parser now runs almost twice as fast as before thanks to a simple trick to avoid the boundary check for most loops.

The easy handle was 4256 bytes large two months ago, it is now 3064 bytes. Almost 40% trimmed off. One of these structs is allocated for every concurrent transfer done with libcurl.

There is also one multi handle allocated for each set of transfer. This struct shrunk from 900 bytes to 656: 37%.

The connectdata struct that is allocated once per connection libcurl handles, went down from 824 to 656 bytes: slightly over 40%.

For the test case where we count all allocations necessary for the curl tool to download a single 512MB file over clear text HTTP://, it went down from 100 to 96 used allocations. Not too exciting perhaps but it is now really hard to squeeze this further!

Mostly thanks to the decreased struct sizes mentioned above, this use case of a single HTTP download now only use 126,875 bytes allocated at peak. Down from 130,622 bytes two months ago. Also quite difficult to trim further.

It should be noted that the download buffer is 102,400 bytes of this amount. If we exclude that buffer from the count, curl is using 15% less memory.

If you think you can speed up any of these functions, it is now very easy to check: the tests are there in the git repository, ready to be invoked by anyone!

items.title: Zero-day exploit completely defeats default Windows 11 BitLocker protections
items.content:
A zero-day exploit circulating online allows people with physical access to a Windows 11 system to bypass default BitLocker protections and gain complete access to an encrypted drive within seconds.

The exploit, named YellowKey, was published earlier this week by a researcher who goes by the alias Nightmare-Eclipse. It reliably bypasses default Windows 11 deployments of BitLocker, the full-volume encryption protection Microsoft provides to make disk contents off-limits to anyone without the decryption key, which is stored in a secured piece of hardware known as a trusted platform module (TPM). BitLocker is a mandatory protection for many organizations, including those that contract with governments.

When one disk volume manipulates another

The core of the YellowKey exploit is a custom-made FsTx folder. Online documentation of this folder is hard to find. As explained later, the directory associated with the file fstx.dll appears to involve what Microsoft calls the transactional NTFS , which allows developers to have “transactional atomicity” for file operations in transactions with a single file, multiple files, or ones that span multiple sources.

The steps for carrying out the bypass are simple:

Copy the custom FsTx folder from the Nightmare-Eclipse exploit page to an NTFS- or FAT-formatted USB drive

Connect the USB drive to the BitLocker-protected device

Boot up the device and immediately press and hold down the [Ctrl] key

There are at least two ways to accomplish the third step. One way is to boot into Windows, hold down the [Shift] key, click on the power icon, and click restart. Another is to power on the device and restart it as soon as Windows starts booting.

In either case, a command (CMD.EXE) prompt appears. The prompt has full access to the entire drive contents, allowing an attacker to copy, modify, or delete them. In a normal Windows Recovery flow, the attacker would need to enter a BitLocker recovery key. Somehow, the YellowKey exploit bypasses this safeguard. Multiple researchers, including Kevin Beaumont and Will Dormann , have confirmed the exploit works as described here.

It’s unclear what in the custom FsTx folder causes the bypass. Dormann said that it appears to be related to Transactional NTFS, which itself uses command-log file system under the hood. Dormann further noted that by looking at the Windows fstx.dll, one will see code that explicitly looks for \System Volume Information\FsTx in the FsTxFindSessions() function.”

The contents of this FsTx directory used in the YellowKey exploit reveal no strings related to RecoverySimulation.ini. It does, however, show the files and paths \??\C:\Windows\win.ini and

\??\X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini, “where X:\Windows\System32\winpeshl.ini is what controls what WinRE [Windows Recovery] does when it fires up.”

Dormann, who is a senior principal vulnerability analyst at Tharros Labs, continued:

But what’s intriguing to me is: Why can the presence a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume affect the contents of ANOTHER VOLUME when it’s replayed? 🤔

In a normal WinRE session, you have a X:\Windows\System32 directory that has a winpeshl.ini file in it:

However, with the YellowKey exploit, it looks like Transactional NTFS bits on a USB Drive are able to delete the winpeshl.ini file on ANOTHER DRIVE (X:). And we get a cmd.exe prompt, with bitlocker unlocked instead of the expected Windows Recovery environment. While the TPM-only Bitlocker bypass is indeed interesting, I think the buried lede here is that a \System Volume Information\FsTx directory on one volume has the ability to modify the contents of another volume when it is replayed. To me, this in and of itself sounds like a vulnerability.

A Microsoft representative declined to answer questions sent by email about the reported vulnerability other than to say the company is investigating.

items.title: Ukraine's Zelenskyy Claims Strikes on Russian Data Centers Silenced Social Media Bots
items.content:
The ongoing Russo-Ukrainian war has mixed the digital and the kinetic in unprecedented and  often terrifying ways, including widespread use of suicide drones , software orchestration of the front lines, and the weaponization of commercial ad data. So it’s hardly surprising that Ukraine has struck data centers run by Russia-based tech giant Yandex (sort of a Facebook/Google/Uber hybrid) three times in the last few days. The most recent  strike, on Oct. 11, reportedly completely disabled a facility in the Vladimir region east of Moscow.

The result was widespread outages of Russian internet services, both within and outside the country. According to Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy, the result was also to near-instantly silence armies of pro-Russian troll bots on social media.

“When we started responding to Russia’s operation against our data centers and when our strikes reached Yandex data centers, it suddenly became a little easier to breathe on many social media platforms,” Zelenskyy told attendees at the Warsaw Security Forum by video link, according to Euronews .

“A lot of people, a lot of people noticed it, and there was less hate, less division and fewer provocations because there were fewer bots,” he added. “And it’s pretty clear where those bots were coming from… If they disappeared when Yandex went offline, this proves again and again that Europe is not the source of the problems.”

Euronews noted that Cloudflare data did appear to show a huge decrease (94%) in automated traffic originating from Yandex on Sunday compared to the average throughout the second half of September. That said, automated traffic is a huge umbrella that includes everything from search crawlers to uptime-monitoring tools.

Euronews also noted that social media users in other countries, like Germany, the UK, and US, also claimed to witness a decrease in bots; this was apparently based on vibes. Online “prediction market” Polymarket also tweeted that “Activity on several major U.S. political subreddits plunges following attacks on Russian data centers,” though that assertion didn’t come with evidence.

Insisting that online rivals are secretly bots is a time-honored posting tactic, one of the few bipartisan ones left—it’s pretty hard to find a front-page Reddit thread that doesn’t have at least a couple comments insisting that “the bots are really out today.” Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty (RFE/RL), a U.S. government-funded broadcaster that primarily serves foreign audiences, noted that technical experts have pointed out the supposed drop in automated traffic is from Yandex’s own search crawler hitting websites with AS13238 HTTP requests. As a result, it does not indicate anything about the broader volume of Russian internet traffic or what it contains.

Finally, that stat only accounts for Russian web traffic that’s already been categorized as automated. Russian cyber adversaries would presumably make at least some kind of cursory effort to obfuscate their traffic, including by locating hosts in other countries where the traffic is less likely to be recognized as Russian in the first place.

Some of the claims appear to conflate data centers with Russian “troll farms” such as the Internet Research Agency (IRA), which became well-known following a 2015 expose . The IRA operated out of a St. Petersburg office building, not a datacenter operated by Yandex. Nor does there appear to be any particular reason the IRA would require an inordinate amount of network resources.

In reality, facilities like the IRA’s or scammer compounds in Myanmar are usually described as operating more like clickbait factories or digital sweatshops than sophisticated, high-tech operations. In other words: cheap labor and automation. One Latvian influence operation that specializes in MAGA content for U.S. conservatives reportedly pays subcontractors in poor countries across the world to clip videos.

Apple unveils the new Apple TV 4K, supercharged by Siri AI

A more capable and conversational Siri, faster performance, and an even more immersive home theater setup elevate the entertainment experience

The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, which transforms how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows; faster performance; and an even more immersive home theater experience.

CUPERTINO, CALIFORNIA Apple today announced the next generation of Apple TV 4K , delivering its most immersive home theater experience yet. The new Apple TV 4K features Siri AI, an entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, transforming how users search for, discover, and enjoy their favorite movies and TV shows through a full-screen Siri AI experience. 1 With built-in far-field microphones, Apple TV 4K also lets users talk to Siri completely hands-free. 2

The new Apple TV 4K delivers even faster performance and, when paired with four HomePod mini 2 or HomePod (2nd generation) speakers, unlocks the most immersive home theater surround sound setup Apple has ever offered. As a home hub, Apple TV 4K also makes managing the smart home easier than ever, with Apple Intelligence-generated camera activity descriptions and summarized notifications in the Home app, and control of accessories and scenes. 3

The new Apple TV 4K can be pre-ordered starting today, with availability beginning November 13.

“The new Apple TV 4K is our most immersive home theater experience yet,” said Bob Borchers, Apple’s vice president of Worldwide Product Marketing. “With Siri AI, finding something to watch becomes a full-screen, conversational experience, and with built-in far-field microphones, it’s completely hands-free. Pair it with HomePod for the best surround sound setup we’ve ever offered, and it makes managing your Apple Home accessories easier than ever. Now, alongside HomeView, HomePod mini 2, and Apple Home Collection, it’s part of the most connected Apple Home we’ve ever built.”

An Entirely New Version of Siri Powered by Apple Intelligence

Apple TV 4K brings Siri AI to the living room with a rich, full-screen experience. An entirely new version of Siri powered by the next generation of Apple Intelligence, Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment. Users can simply ask Siri “What Apple TV shows won at the Emmy Awards this year?” and see beautiful poster art pulled directly from the Apple TV app, along with relevant suggestions like “More award-winning comedies” to keep exploring. While watching, users can ask Siri AI follow-up questions and tap into Siri AI’s broad world knowledge to go deeper into a show, asking things like “Where was Pluribus filmed?” or “Is this appropriate for a 15-year-old?” Responses appear in a compact, subtle overlay, providing helpful information when viewers ask while keeping them immersed in the action. With an Apple Intelligence-enabled iPhone, Siri AI on Apple TV 4K can now tap into a user’s personal context to answer requests like “Play the show Alinda recommended.”

Siri AI is a profoundly more capable and conversational assistant with personal context understanding, broad world knowledge, and the ability to take even more systemwide app actions, making it effortless to find entertainment.

A Fully Hands-Free Experience with Far-Field Microphones

The new Apple TV 4K features three far-field microphones, letting users control what they’re watching and discover new shows completely hands-free. Advanced echo cancellation intelligently isolates a user’s voice from background sound to deliver crystal-clear “Hey Siri” or “Siri” recognition, even while audio is playing.

Fridges in French supermarkets hit by cyber attack

16 hours ago Share Save Add as preferred on Google

Hundreds of French supermarkets have been hit by a cyber attack that caused their fridges and freezers to heat up, spoiling fresh and frozen food estimated to be worth millions of euros.

Hackers gained control of the software that regulates the temperatures of the refrigeration units, forcing some to warm to 50C (120F) overnight, according to one supermarket chain affected.

The chief executive of Coopérative U said several of its supermarkets had been hit by the "extremely serious and unprecedented" attack.

More than 100 of the chain's supermarkets were targeted, while 180 stores from Intermarché and its Netto brand were affected, with a spokesman saying that another 100 shops were urgently disconnected from the internet to prevent the same thing happening to them.

Other major food retailers including Carrefour, Monoprix and E.Leclerc were also hit by the attack, which targeted software provided by Danish engineering firm Danfoss.

The software allows retailers to manage their cold units remotely.

Normally, supermarket freezers go through a short period of defrosting overnight, in which temperatures rise slightly. But the hackers ordered the units to heat up and stay hot, although Danfoss did not confirm any reports about just how warm the fridges and freezers could become in that process.

Danfoss said the affected cold units were older models whose security software could not be updated to ward off a risk they had identified.

The firm added in a statement that it had "long advised" businesses to keep supported systems up to date.

"Reliable refrigeration is critical to our customers' operations, and we remain committed to supporting our customers and helping them maintain secure and reliable systems they are used to."

The full scale of the attack is unclear, but figures supplied by individual chains suggest about 400 stores were affected out of 15,000 or so overall in France.

Carrefour said fridges in 80 of its 6,000 stores were hacked, while Monoprix said 5% of its 400-plus stores had been hit, with food removed from sale if its condition could not be guaranteed.

In a statement to the BBC, Mousquetaires Group - which owns Intermarché and Netto - said some fresh and frozen food display units remained out of service on Monday afternoon.

The stores had "taken all necessary precautions to remove the products from these units", it said, adding that staff were working to restock the shelves "as soon as possible".

Intermarché said its fridges had heated up to 50C for six hours overnight into Monday, and the retailer had thrown away all the affected food to avoid health risks, the Reuters news agency reported.

As a result of the attack, managers arriving at branches of several supermarket chains on Monday morning were hit by a wave of hot air from the freezers. In some places there were even small fires.

French broadcaster BFMTV published an image showing a freezer in an ice cream aisle displaying a temperature of 26.5C.

Two supermarkets in the Alsace region reported losses of €270,000 (£228,000) between them, the broadcaster added, meaning the nationwide total could run into the millions.

French prosecutors have opened a specific cyber-crime investigation into the incident, which the Paris prosecutor's office called a "large-scale cyber-attack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France".

European Food Commissioner Christophe Hansen condemned the hack in a post on X and added: "Food security requires more attention at all levels. Because the weaponisation of food has become a reality."

In a post on X, Coopérative chief executive Dominique Schelcher said staff were "fully mobilised, in co-ordination with refrigeration specialists, to restore the situation as quickly as possible".

items.title: NetBSD may have found a new role: The AI-free FOSS OS
items.content:
NetBSD may have found a new role: The AI-free FOSS OS

Increasing awareness and adoption, followed by increasing donations

Pigeon-powered internet packet goes under the hammer at Christie's

Raspberry Pi Desktop catches up with Debian 13 after 4-year wait

OpenAI dots inspire open source imitators amid technical difficulties

COSMIC shuts the door on AI code as GNOME debates letting bug reports in

Only the finest Swedish Bork will do for Stockholm station

NetBSD seems to be thriving of late: as the Linux world goes pro-AI, some of the AI-averse are turning to this explicitly AI-free project.

The NetBSD project’s Mastodon feed reports that it received a record 120 donations last month, and it has far exceeded its target:

“We received $120,282 USD in total. Naturally, this has completely filled up our donations target bar which was set at $50,000. Time to fund some projects!”

It’s a welcome contrast to the usual stories of under-funded FOSS projects, and it follows a visible uptick in people asking about NetBSD in the FOSS Unix groups we read, ever since Emperor Penguin Torvalds said that Linux was not an anti-AI project back in July, and the following month, the Debian project polled its developers on AI use, and they chose to permit AI-generated contributions .

This is the moderate, centrist stance. The most recent Ubuntu Summit was heavily AI-flavored . The heads of Red Hat Global Engineering sent out a memo about transitioning to an Agentic Software Development Lifecycle . But once it’s in the kernel, then no distro can totally avoid it. This stance is profoundly offputting to those who prefer hand-crafted code.

Last week, the Reg FOSS desk attended the Open Source Summit Europe in Prague . This event reflects the tendencies of the increasingly mainstream open-source world: Linux is pretty much the only OS in evidence, although many attendees tote around (and present from) MacBooks, and both Microsoft and Windows were visible. The event overlaps with Embedded Linux Conference , so the Zephyr RTOS was also visible on some robots and other gadgets.

The Open Source Summit gives the overall impression that Linux is the only general-purpose FOSS OS. We saw no mention at all of any of the BSDs; indeed, when we mentioned NetBSD, some of the folks from Let’s Encrypt looked puzzled and asked us “What’s ‘net bee ess dee’?” Sadly, this is probably a reasonably fair representation of its presence at the event and in the FOSS mainstream. For us, the single most dominant theme in the talks, the materials, the stands, and even the T-shirts was AI. It’s everywhere, and every exhibitor was keen to talk about how they’re using AI, deploying AI, scaling AI, or managing AI.

The louder the noise about AI gets, the stronger grows the aversion of those of us who actively wish to avoid it. The NetBSD project, on the other hand, came out early and strongly: it banned AI-generated code back in 2024, just a month after the project celebrated its 30th anniversary .

This vulture attended the project’s talk at that year’s FOSDEM: NetBSD 10: Thirty years, still going strong ! . As ever, the question of differentiation between the BSDs, and between Linux and the BSDs, came up.

NetBSD’s slogan is “Of course it runs NetBSD,”  but in 2024, its ubiquity was looking threatened: Linux is comparable, and FreeBSD boast close integration with ZFS, Linux-compatible Podman containers, and more.

The following year, though, FreeBSD 15 appeared, dropping support for 32-bit x86 (and 32-bit POWER). Debian 13 dropped x86-32 too , as well as MIPS CPU support. That year, the RHEL 10 release went further: it not only requires 64-bit x86, it demands x86-64-v3. This cut off so many older machines, it forced CERN to start switching to Debian .

From within the BSD world, the differences between the various projects are fairly clear. NetBSD is minimal, highly portable, and takes great pride in its very friendly, welcoming community. We can personally attest to this:…

온오프라인을 가리지 않고 무분별하게 벌어지는 각종 프라이버시 침해 및 스토킹과 이에 대한 예방, 방지 및 사후 대응, 더 나아가서 개인정보 탈취 및 감시용 스파이웨어, 스토커웨어, 바이러스, 원격 조종, 추적기 등 악성코드를 통한 해킹과 스토킹 등 개인정보 침해 공격 방지와 온오프라인 프라이버시 보호를 위한 각종 다양한 지식정보를 공유하는 갤러리입니다.

위임 절차는 신고 게시판 > 분류 선택에 [매니저 위임]으로 위임받을 이용자가 직접 신청하면 진행됩니다. 검토 결과 운영에 적합하다고 판단되는 회원에게 매니저 권한을 위임하게 됩니다.

부매니저가 장기간(최소 10일 이상) 부재 시 부재중으로 표시되며, 매니저에 의해 해임될 수 있습니다.

식별 코드 기준으로 당일 글 10개, 댓글 20개 작성 시 대왕디시콘을 3일간 사용할 수 있습니다.

즐겨찾기 폴더 추가는 즐겨찾기 on 후 우측의 폴더 아이콘을 터치하여 추가할 수 있습니다.
